definition.text: A trade arrangement meant to help producers in developing countries get sustainable and fair conditions, by paying higher prices and raising social and environmental standards.

facts.text: It focuses on commodities exported from poorer to richer countries, notably handicrafts, coffee, cocoa, wine, sugar, fruit, flowers and gold.
The current movement took shape in Europe in the 1960s, and sales only took off once Fairtrade certification labels arrived.
Fairtrade labelling uses independent audits of producers and traders, and the guarantee of a minimum price is its most distinctive feature.
In 2011 more than 1.2 million farmers and workers in over 60 countries took part in Fairtrade International's system.
Coffee is the most established fair trade commodity.
Direct trade, which skips certification overhead, is proposed as an alternative.

definition.text: Extra money that buyers of fair trade goods pay to producer groups, who decide democratically how to spend it.

facts.text: Under Fairtrade the premium goes to the cooperative rather than directly to individual producers.
Groups often spend it on public goods that government fails to provide, such as environmental projects, schools and water projects.
In 2011 Fairtrade International's system paid €65 million in premiums to producers for community development.

title: Criticism of fair trade

definition.text: The debate over whether fair trade actually benefits poor producers, given studies that find both gains and little effect.

facts.text: A 2015 study found producer benefits close to zero because of an oversupply of certification.
Little of the extra retail price may reach farmers: one estimate found US exporters received only 2% of a US$5 per pound retail premium on coffee.
Because coffee demand is highly inelastic, economists argue higher fair trade output can push down prices for the many non-certified farmers.
A study in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found it meets many of its goals, though on a modest scale.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether fair trade raises producers' incomes and working conditions or mostly benefits intermediaries.
